posts.title: FlashAttention: Attention Was Never FLOP-Bound
posts.subtitle: The slow part of attention was never the math — it was shuttling a giant matrix in and out of GPU memory.
posts.summary: FlashAttention computes exact softmax attention without ever materializing the full N×N score matrix in slow GPU memory, by tiling the computation into blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM. It's the same math, same output — just radically less memory traffic, which is what was actually slow.

slides.title: Same Attention, Same Answer, 2-4x Faster
slides.body: FlashAttention doesn't approximate attention — it computes the exact same result as standard attention, just without the memory bottleneck that made the naive version slow.

slides.title: The Real Bottleneck Was Memory Traffic, Not Math
slides.body: Modern GPUs can do far more FLOPs per second than they can move bytes between HBM (high-bandwidth memory) and SRAM (on-chip cache). Standard attention is dominated by the latter.
bullets: Standard attention computes the full N×N score matrix (QKᵗ), writes it to HBM, reads it back for softmax, writes it again, reads it for the final matmul with V
That's several full read/write passes over an N×N matrix — for a 16K-token sequence, that matrix alone is 256M entries
GPUs are compute-rich but bandwidth-starved: an A100 can do ~19.5 TFLOPs/s but only move ~2TB/s between HBM and SRAM
Attention is 'memory-bound,' not 'compute-bound' — speeding up the matmul doesn't help if you're waiting on memory transfers

slides.title: Tiling: Never Materialize the Full Matrix
slides.body: FlashAttention fuses the whole attention computation into one GPU kernel that keeps everything in fast on-chip SRAM, block by block.
bullets: Split Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in SRAM (which is tiny — tens of KB per streaming multiprocessor — but ~10x faster than HBM)
For each block of Q, loop over blocks of K and V, computing partial attention scores entirely on-chip
Never write the N×N score matrix back to HBM — only the final output and softmax statistics leave the chip
Result: memory traffic drops from O(N²) to O(N) with respect to sequence length

slides.title: The Trick That Makes Tiling Exact: Online Softmax
slides.body: Softmax normally needs the full row of scores before it can divide by their sum — which seems to require having the whole matrix. Online softmax avoids that.
bullets: Keep a running maximum and running sum as each new block of scores arrives, rescaling the accumulated output so far when a new, larger max shows up
This gives the mathematically exact same softmax output as computing it over the full row at once — no approximation
It's the same trick used in streaming/numerically-stable softmax implementations, just applied block-by-block inside the fused kernel
Because it's exact, FlashAttention changes nothing about model quality — it's a systems optimization, not an architecture change

slides.title: Standard Attention vs. FlashAttention

rows: O(N²) — full score matrix read/written repeatedly
O(N) — only blocks, output, and softmax stats touch HBM
Compute (much closer to GPU's FLOP ceiling)
Memory blows up quickly past a few thousand tokens
Same memory budget supports far longer sequences

slides.title: Why This Mattered for Longer Context Windows
slides.body: Picture training a model with a 16K-token context on a fixed GPU memory budget.
bullets: With standard attention, the N×N intermediate matrix for 16K tokens alone can exceed available memory before you even count activations and gradients — training either OOMs or forces a much smaller batch size
With FlashAttention, that intermediate matrix is never materialized, so the same GPU memory budget comfortably fits the longer sequence
This is a direct, practical reason long-context models became feasible to train without just throwing more GPUs at the problem
FlashAttention-2 later improved on this further by restructuring the work split across GPU thread blocks for better parallelism, pushing GPU utilization meaningfully closer to peak throughput

slides.title: Where It Doesn't Help — and What It Isn't
slides.body: FlashAttention is not a universal speedup, and it's not the same thing as other attention-related tricks you'll see mentioned alongside it.
bullets: For very short sequences, the N×N matrix was never big enough to be the bottleneck — gains shrink accordingly
It's an exact method, not an approximation — don't confuse it with sparse or linear-attention methods that trade quality for speed on even longer sequences
It optimizes the attention operation during training/prefill; it is not the same as PagedAttention, which manages KV-cache memory during inference — the two are complementary, not competitors
Implementations are tuned to specific GPU architectures (SRAM size, thread block layout); porting to new hardware generations requires re-tuning, not just a recompile

slides.title: The Core Idea, Stripped Down
bullets: Identify the real bottleneck: attention was memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, on modern GPUs
Fuse the computation into one kernel and tile it so intermediate results never leave fast on-chip memory
Use online softmax to keep the tiled computation mathematically exact — no quality tradeoff
The payoff compounds: faster training and, crucially, enough memory headroom to train on much longer sequences

questions.prompt: Why was standard attention slow on GPUs, according to FlashAttention's core insight?
options: The matrix multiplications involved too many floating-point operations for the GPU to handle
It was bottlenecked by moving the N×N score matrix repeatedly between slow HBM and fast on-chip SRAM, not by raw compute
GPUs cannot execute softmax efficiently in any form
The attention mechanism required more parameters than the GPU could store
questions.explanation: GPUs have far more compute throughput (FLOPs/s) than memory bandwidth. Standard attention repeatedly reads and writes the full N×N matrix to HBM, making it memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.

questions.prompt: What does 'online softmax' let FlashAttention do?
options: Approximate the softmax to save time, trading a small amount of accuracy for speed
Skip the softmax step entirely for long sequences
Compute the exact softmax incrementally over blocks, using a running max and sum, without ever needing the full row of scores at once
Run softmax on a separate, specialized accelerator chip
questions.explanation: Online softmax keeps a running maximum and sum, rescaling the accumulated result as new blocks arrive. This produces the exact same output as computing softmax over the full row — it's a reformulation, not an approximation.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes FlashAttention from PagedAttention?
options: They solve the same problem and are interchangeable
FlashAttention approximates attention scores; PagedAttention computes them exactly
FlashAttention optimizes the attention computation itself (e.g., during training/prefill); PagedAttention manages how KV-cache memory is allocated during inference — they're complementary
PagedAttention replaced FlashAttention as the newer, strictly better technique
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is about computing attention without materializing the full score matrix. PagedAttention is about efficiently paging the KV cache during generation. Systems commonly use both together, since they address different parts of the pipeline.

posts.title: Token Bucket vs. Sliding Window: Picking a Rate Limiter
posts.subtitle: The same '100 requests per minute' rule can mean very different things to your backend, depending on which algorithm enforces it.
posts.summary: Rate limiting algorithms trade off memory, accuracy, and burst tolerance differently. Fixed windows are simple but leak bursts at the boundary; token bucket allows controlled bursts with O(1) memory; sliding window log is precise but costly; sliding window counters split the difference — and none of it works right in a distributed system without shared state.

slides.title: Not All Rate Limiters Enforce the Same Rule
slides.body: "100 requests per minute" sounds like one rule — but fixed-window, sliding-window, and token-bucket implementations enforce meaningfully different real-world limits.

slides.title: The Fixed Window's Boundary Burst
slides.body: The simplest rate limiter — a counter that resets every minute — has a well-known flaw at window edges.
bullets: A client sends 100 requests in the last second of window 1, then another 100 in the first second of window 2
Each window individually stayed within its 100-request cap — but the backend just took 200 requests in roughly 2 seconds
That's a 2x burst over the intended average rate, purely from the reset boundary — not from any bug in the counting logic
Fixed windows are still popular because they're O(1) memory and trivial to implement — the burst risk is a known, acceptable tradeoff for many APIs

slides.title: Token Bucket: Bound the Burst, Not Just the Average
slides.body: A bucket holds up to N tokens and refills at a steady rate; each request consumes one token.
bullets: Bucket capacity N caps the maximum burst size; refill rate R (tokens/sec) caps the long-run average rate
If the bucket is full, a client can legitimately fire N requests instantly — that's a feature, not a leak, because it's an explicit, bounded allowance
State per client is just two numbers: current token count and last-refill timestamp — O(1) memory regardless of traffic volume
This is the algorithm behind most cloud API gateways' documented 'burst limit' vs. 'sustained rate' distinction

slides.title: Sliding Window: Log vs. Counter
slides.body: Two ways to avoid the fixed-window boundary problem without token bucket's bucket semantics.
bullets: Sliding window log: store the timestamp of every request in the trailing window; on each new request, drop timestamps older than the window and count what's left — perfectly accurate, but memory grows with request volume per client
Sliding window counter: keep only two fixed-window counts (current and previous), and estimate the sliding count as a weighted blend based on how far into the current window you are
The counter approach uses O(1) memory like fixed window, but smooths out the boundary burst to a close approximation instead of eliminating it exactly
Most production systems (e.g., Cloudflare's public rate-limiting writeups) use the sliding window counter precisely because log-based accuracy isn't worth the per-client memory cost at scale

slides.title: Four Algorithms, Side by Side
Walking Through a Burst Client
slides.body: A client is capped at 1,000 requests/hour and sends 950 requests in the first minute, then goes idle.
bullets: Fixed window: all 950 requests pass (under the 1,000 cap for that hour) — then the client can send another 950 the moment the hour rolls over, producing a visible 2-request-storm pattern at the boundary

Token bucket (capacity 1,000, refill ~0.28 tokens/sec): the 950 requests drain the bucket to 50 tokens; the client must now wait for tokens to trickle back in before bursting again — no hour-boundary cliff
Sliding window counter: correctly reflects that 950 of the last 60 seconds' worth of allowance is used, smoothly decaying rather than resetting all at once
This is why APIs that explicitly advertise a 'burst' allowance (vs. just an hourly cap) are almost always using token bucket under the hood

slides.title: The Part Every Algorithm Gets Wrong in Production: Distribution
slides.body: All four algorithms above assume one process holding the counter. Real backends don't.
bullets: Behind a load balancer with 10 gateway instances, each running its own in-memory limiter, a client can get ~10x the intended limit by spreading requests across instances
Fixing this requires shared state — typically Redis — so every instance checks and decrements the same counter or bucket

That introduces a race condition: two instances can both read 'token available' before either writes 'token consumed,' double-spending the last token — the fix is an atomic operation (Redis `INCR` with `EXPIRE`, or a Lua script for token bucket's two-step check-and-decrement)
Don't use naive per-instance in-memory rate limiting behind multiple servers and assume the limit holds — it won't, by roughly the instance count

slides.title: Picking One
bullets: Need simplicity and can tolerate occasional small bursts: fixed window
Need to advertise an explicit burst allowance on top of a sustained rate: token bucket
Need the smoothest approximation at O(1) memory with no explicit burst policy: sliding window counter
Running behind more than one server instance: none of the above work without shared, atomically-updated state

questions.prompt: What is the core flaw in a naive fixed-window rate limiter?
options: It uses too much memory per client to be practical
It cannot be implemented without a database
Requests clustered at the boundary between two windows can let a client send up to roughly 2x the intended rate in a short span
It cannot support any burst traffic at all
questions.explanation: Because each window's counter resets independently, a client can max out the end of one window and the start of the next, briefly doubling the effective rate — even though neither window individually exceeded its cap.

questions.prompt: What makes token bucket different from a sliding window counter in how it treats bursts?
options: Token bucket forbids all bursts; sliding window counter allows unlimited bursts
Token bucket explicitly allows a bounded burst up to the bucket's capacity, by design; sliding window counter only approximates a steady rate and has no explicit burst allowance
They are mathematically identical algorithms with different names
Sliding window counter requires more memory per client than token bucket
questions.explanation: Token bucket treats burst capacity as a first-class, intentional parameter — a full bucket can legally be drained all at once. Sliding window counter just smooths the rate estimate; it isn't designed to grant deliberate bursts.

questions.prompt: Why does rate limiting break down behind multiple load-balanced server instances without extra work?
options: Because token bucket only works on a single CPU core
Because each instance would track its own separate counter/bucket in memory, letting a client effectively multiply its limit by the number of instances it gets routed across
Because sliding window algorithms are incompatible with load balancers entirely
Because HTTPS prevents rate limiting counters from being shared
questions.explanation: If each instance keeps its own in-memory state, a client spread across N instances can get roughly N times the intended limit. Fixing this requires centralized, atomically-updated shared state (e.g., Redis) so all instances enforce one real counter.

posts.title: Anthropic's New Defense Cuts AI Model Theft by 90-99%
posts.subtitle: How Claude fights back against networks stealing its reasoning to train rival models
posts.summary: Anthropic detailed a three-layer defense against 'distillation attacks' — covert campaigns that harvest Claude's reasoning transcripts to train competing models. Early data shows a 10-100x+ drop in extracted reasoning tokens, with a sub-0.1% false-positive rate.

slides.title: Someone Is Mining Claude's Reasoning to Train Rival Models
slides.body: On Oct 12, 2026, Anthropic published how it fights 'distillation attacks' — large-scale, covert campaigns that extract a model's reasoning to train another company's model without permission.

slides.title: What Distillers Actually Want: The Reasoning, Not the Answer
slides.body: A final answer is cheap to imitate. The step-by-step reasoning that produced it is what's valuable — and expensive to fake.
bullets: Distillers run thousands of fraudulent accounts to harvest Claude's extended-thinking transcripts at scale
Anthropic found requests sent to Moonshot's Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude — including one tied to a user believed affiliated with China's PLA, analyzing CCTV footage of an individual
Zhipu's GLM-5.3, assessed by CAISI as the most cyber-capable open-weights model released so far, is cited as a case where distilled capability outran the safeguards wrapped around it

slides.title: Three Layers: Lock the Reasoning, Classify the Attempts, Throttle the Repeaters
slides.body: The defense doesn't rely on one trick — it stacks controls at the account, request, and pattern level.
bullets: 'Preserved thinking' blocks new API accounts (created on/after Aug 31, 2026) from editing Claude's prior reasoning context, closing a proxy-network extraction path — shipped with Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5
On Claude Sonnet 5.5, raw reasoning transcripts are visible only to the organization whose own request produced them

A two-stage classifier (built on Anthropic's constitutional-classifiers research) runs on the most capable GA models, catching tactics like asking Claude to 'translate' or re-emit its prior reasoning in disguised tags
Accounts showing persistent extraction attempts get stricter rate limits or outright bans — often within two hours of a campaign starting

slides.title: The Numbers: Harder to Steal, Barely Harder to Use Honestly

rows: 10-100x+ lower; some days too small to measure
Model trained on summarized vs. full reasoning (SWE-bench Verified)
Reduction in data harvested by distillers

slides.title: Worked Example: Catching a Proxy-Network Campaign
slides.body: A ring of accounts, created in bulk after a prior ban wave, starts issuing high-volume requests designed to elicit long reasoning chains, then strips and reformats the output to train a separate model.
bullets: The two-stage classifier flags the pattern — not a single request, but the shape of repeated extraction-style prompting across the account cluster
Flagged accounts face throttling first, then bans if the pattern persists — most within two hours of the campaign starting
Since Sept 24, 2026, Anthropic charges for requests its safeguards block before Claude even responds, including in distillation cases, removing the 'free scouting' incentive

slides.title: The Cost of Being Careful
slides.body: Every defense here trades something — Anthropic is explicit about it rather than claiming a free lunch.
bullets: Preserved thinking requires some legitimate developers to update integrations that previously edited prior context
Under 0.1% of benign requests still get blocked by the classifier — and are now billed anyway
Anthropic says it hasn't yet seen a highly sophisticated, persistent attempt to bypass the full stack — this is explicitly framed as an ongoing cat-and-mouse game, not a solved problem

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Model theft isn't just an IP problem — Anthropic frames it as a safety and national-security one, since distilled capability can arrive without the original model's safeguards attached.
bullets: Reasoning transcripts, not outputs, are the real target of distillation attacks
Defense-in-depth beat any single filter: account controls + classifiers + rate-limiting, stacked
Anthropic is publishing the approach specifically because industry incentives often discourage building these defenses at all
Expect this to keep evolving — attackers can still shift traffic to less-protected providers

questions.prompt: What do distillation attacks primarily try to extract from a model like Claude?
options: Its training data
Its final answers only
Its step-by-step reasoning transcripts
Its API rate limits
questions.explanation: Final answers are easy to imitate; the valuable (and costly-to-fake) asset is the chain of reasoning that produced them — so that's what distillers specifically harvest at scale.

questions.prompt: In Anthropic's comparison, a model trained on SUMMARIZED reasoning scored 71.8% on SWE-bench Verified. What did a model trained on FULL reasoning score?
questions.explanation: Full reasoning transcripts transferred meaningfully more capability (80.4% vs 71.8%), which is exactly why distillers want the raw reasoning and not just summaries or outputs.

questions.prompt: Why does Anthropic treat distillation as a safety issue, not just a competitive one?
options: It increases Anthropic's cloud compute costs
Distilled capability can reach frontier-level performance without the original model's safeguards attached, as in the GLM-5.3 case
It violates a trademark
It only affects pricing, not capability
questions.explanation: Anthropic cites GLM-5.3 — assessed as the most cyber-capable open-weights model released so far — as evidence that distilled capability can outrun the safety wrapper around it, enabling misuse in biology or cybersecurity.

references.title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks

posts.title: RSI-Anything: Predicting Outcomes Before Paying for Real Feedback
posts.subtitle: A world model that lets self-improving AI filter its own ideas before the expensive check
posts.summary: RSI-Anything (arXiv 2610.13912) adds a predictive world model in front of costly real-world feedback — compiling code, running lab experiments, operating a GUI — so an improving policy only pays for evaluation on its most promising candidates. Reported gains span code repair, lab planning, GUI control, and reaction optimization.

slides.title: The Bottleneck in Self-Improving AI Isn't Ideas — It's Checking Them
slides.body: RSI-Anything (Taoyong Cui, Ling Yang, Wanli Ouyang, Pheng Ann Heng et al., arXiv 2610.13912, Oct 9 2026) targets the cost of real-world feedback in recursive self-improvement.

slides.title: Real Feedback Is Expensive, So You Can't Just Brute-Force Self-Improvement
slides.body: A self-improving agent wants to try many candidate actions or policy tweaks — but every real evaluation (a compiler run, a wet-lab experiment, a GUI action) costs time or money.
bullets: Running everything through full external evaluation doesn't scale as the policy iterates
But skipping evaluation means the policy can't tell a good idea from a bad one
The paper's framing: use a learned world model as a cheap filter, and save real feedback for only the candidates worth it

slides.title: The Loop: Propose → Predict → Verify → Pay for the Best Only
slides.body: Built on JEPA-Anything, the predictive world model sits between the policy and the real environment.
bullets: The policy proposes multiple candidate actions or revisions
A world model predicts each candidate's likely outcome — no real execution yet
A verifier discards clearly invalid or low-value candidates based on those predictions

Only the surviving high-utility candidates get costly external evaluation; those real observations update the policy — and, when the world model's predictions start drifting from reality, trigger a world-model adaptation step too

slides.title: Reported Gains Across Three Very Different Domains
slides.body: Numbers are the authors' own reported results (not independently replicated at time of writing).

rows: Code repair (CodeContests, static verifier → full pipeline)
Reaction optimization (same 40-experiment budget vs. Bayesian opt.)

slides.title: Worked Example: Fixing a Bug Without Running the Test Suite Every Time
slides.body: In the code-repair setting, a coding model (reported as ReasonFlux-Coder-7B) proposes several candidate patches for a failing test.
bullets: Instead of compiling and running the full test suite for every candidate, the world model predicts which patches are likely to pass
Only the most promising patches get a real test run — reported average of about 3.7 real test invocations per task
Over successive rounds, this raised reported success from 26.3% (static verifier alone) to 31.2% (after the world model itself got updated)

slides.title: Read the Numbers Carefully
slides.body: This is a single paper's self-reported results — treat it as a promising direction, not a settled benchmark.
bullets: No independent replication yet; all figures above come from the authors
The world model can become unreliable as the policy evolves past what it was trained to predict — the paper's own fix is to periodically retrain the world model, which is itself a cost
Only three domains were tested (code repair, lab planning, reaction optimization, plus a GUI setting) — 'domain-general' is the claim, not yet an exhaustively proven property

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: A reusable pattern for anyone building self-improving agents: don't pay for real feedback on every idea — predict first, verify cheaply, and reserve expensive evaluation for your best shots.
bullets: World models aren't just for robotics/video generation — here they're a filter that cuts evaluation cost in agentic self-improvement
The same framework reportedly transferred across code, lab science, and GUI control without domain-specific redesign
The adaptation step (updating the world model itself, not just the policy) is what keeps predictions from going stale as the policy improves

questions.prompt: What problem does the world model in RSI-Anything solve?
options: It generates more training data from scratch
It predicts a candidate action's outcome cheaply, before paying for real (expensive) feedback
It replaces the policy entirely
It only works for image generation
questions.explanation: The world model acts as a cheap pre-filter: it predicts outcomes for candidate actions so only the most promising ones need costly real-world evaluation (compiling code, running an experiment, etc.).

questions.prompt: In the code-repair benchmark, what was the reported success rate after the world model itself was adapted, versus using only a static verifier?
questions.explanation: The paper reports 26.3% with a static verifier, 29.2% with predictive selection alone, and 31.2% once the world model was also adapted — each step adding real improvement.

questions.prompt: Why does RSI-Anything sometimes trigger a 'world-model adaptation' step, rather than only updating the policy?
options: To save on GPU memory
Because the world model's predictions can drift and become unreliable as the policy itself evolves
It happens on a fixed schedule unrelated to performance
To reset the policy back to its starting point
questions.explanation: As the policy changes, it visits states the world model wasn't trained on well, so its predictions can degrade — the paper addresses this by adapting the world model itself when reliability drops, not just the policy.

references.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models

posts.title: A2A: The Protocol for Agents Talking to Other Agents
posts.subtitle: MCP connects an agent to tools. A2A connects an agent to another agent it doesn't control.
posts.summary: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol — now under Linux Foundation governance — for autonomous agents built by different teams or vendors to discover each other's capabilities and exchange long-running tasks, without either side seeing the other's internal reasoning.

slides.title: MCP Connects an Agent to Tools. What Connects an Agent to Another Agent?
slides.body: Model Context Protocol standardizes how one agent calls tools and reads resources. Agent2Agent (A2A) standardizes something different: how two independent agents collaborate as peers.

slides.title: Peer Agents Aren't Tools — They're Opaque, Autonomous, and Someone Else's
slides.body: A tool is deterministic and fully specified. A peer agent — maybe built by another company — has its own reasoning you can't inspect and shouldn't need to.
bullets: Before A2A, integrating another company's agent usually meant a one-off, custom API per vendor
A tool call is a single request/response; an agent-to-agent task can run for minutes or hours, with multiple back-and-forth updates
You need to discover what another agent can do and how to authenticate with it — without reading its source or prompts

slides.title: The Core Primitives: Agent Card, Task, and Artifact
slides.body: A2A reached v1.0 in 2026 under Linux Foundation governance, with three supported transports: JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON.
bullets: Agent Card — a JSON manifest published at a well-known URI (/.well-known/agent-card.json) describing an agent's skills, capabilities, and supported auth methods (API key, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, mTLS)
Task — the unit of work sent to another agent; it has a lifecycle (submitted → working → completed/failed) and can run long, with streamed status updates over SSE
Artifact — the structured output a task produces, handed back to the caller once work is done

slides.title: MCP vs. A2A: Different Problems, Often Used Together

rows: The other agent's reasoning stays opaque

slides.title: Worked Example: A Travel Orchestrator That Doesn't Own a Flight Agent
slides.body: An orchestrator agent needs to book a trip but has no flight-search logic of its own.
bullets: It fetches a specialized flight-search agent's Agent Card to learn its skills and required auth
It authenticates per the card's declared method, then submits a Task ('find flights: SFO→NRT, under $900, next week')
The flight agent streams status updates while it works, then returns an Artifact — a structured itinerary — without the orchestrator ever seeing how it searched

slides.title: When A2A Is the Wrong Tool
slides.body: Protocol overhead buys you something specific — don't pay for it when you don't need it.
bullets: Inside a single codebase or team, a direct function call or MCP tool call is simpler than standing up Agent Cards and task lifecycles
Publishing an Agent Card publicly expands your attack surface — it's a discoverable manifest of what your agent can do
A2A adds real complexity (auth negotiation, task state management) that's wasted if you already control both sides of the integration

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: A2A and MCP solve adjacent but distinct problems, and a mature agent stack often uses both.
bullets: MCP = agent to tool. A2A = agent to agent. Don't conflate them
Agent Cards give agents a standard way to advertise capabilities without exposing internals
Tasks and Artifacts make long-running, asynchronous agent collaboration a first-class citizen, not a workaround
Reach for A2A at organizational boundaries — skip it when you already control both ends

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between what MCP and A2A each connect?
options: They are two names for the same protocol
MCP connects an agent to tools/data sources; A2A connects an agent to another agent
MCP is for video, A2A is for text
A2A replaced MCP entirely in 2026
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes an agent's access to tools and resources it effectively owns. A2A standardizes collaboration between independent, autonomous agents that don't share internals.

questions.prompt: Where does an A2A-compliant agent publish what it can do?
options: In its system prompt
A JSON 'Agent Card' manifest at a well-known URI like /.well-known/agent-card.json
Nowhere — capabilities are negotiated verbally at runtime
In a Dockerfile
questions.explanation: The Agent Card is a discoverable JSON manifest describing an agent's skills, capabilities, and supported authentication methods, so other agents can learn how to work with it without inspecting its internals.

questions.prompt: Why might two agents from different companies prefer A2A over a custom one-off API integration?
options: A2A is always faster at the network level
It gives them a standard way to discover capabilities, negotiate auth, and manage long-running tasks — without either side needing to see the other's internal reasoning
Custom APIs are no longer legal
A2A eliminates the need for authentication
questions.explanation: The value of a shared protocol is avoiding a bespoke integration per vendor: standardized discovery (Agent Card), task lifecycle, and auth negotiation let independent agents interoperate as black boxes to each other.

posts.title: StudentSim: Training AI Tutors Without Real Students
posts.subtitle: Personalized LLM student simulators beat GPT-5.4 at predicting real learners — and trained a tutor that human experts preferred.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research built StudentSim, a system that trains one personalized LLM simulator per real student from de-identified records, so AI tutors can be tested and improved without costly human studies. In a chess experiment, using StudentSim as the reward signal for reinforcement learning produced a tutor that hit 90.5% accuracy and was rated best by blind human experts.

slides.title: Can an AI tutor be trained without real students?
slides.body: Microsoft Research's StudentSim builds personalized LLM simulators of individual learners, so tutor-training can run before (or instead of) slow, expensive human studies.

slides.title: Human-in-the-loop tutor testing doesn't scale
slides.body: Improving an AI tutor usually means running real students through it, which is slow and costly. The cheap alternative — prompting an LLM to 'act like a student' — tends to be too capable, flattering the tutor instead of stress-testing it.
bullets: Human studies: slow, expensive, hard to iterate on
Generic prompted 'student' LLMs: too competent, not representative of any real learner
Result: tutors look good in testing, then underperform with actual students

slides.title: One simulator per student, trained in two stages
slides.body: StudentSim trains from publicly available, de-identified learner records. It first learns shared patterns pooled across many students in a domain, then specializes on each individual student's own history.
bullets: Stage 1: pretrain on pooled records across the whole domain (chess, writing, math)
Stage 2: specialize per-student on that learner's own recorded answers
Two-stage design compensates for how little data any single student has
Positioned as a research tool to pre-screen tutors, not a classroom product

slides.title: StudentSimEval: two things a good simulator must do
slides.body: The benchmark spans chess, second-language English writing, and math, and scores each simulator on two axes.
bullets: Behavioral fidelity — does it match THIS student's actual answers on held-out problems?
Guidance responsiveness — does it change its answer after reading tutor feedback?
A simulator can ace one axis and fail the other — both are needed to be useful

slides.title: StudentSim vs. a prompted LLM vs. a chess-specific model
slides.body: In the chess domain, StudentSim beat both a generic prompted LLM and a specialized chess move-predictor — each strong on only one axis.

slides.title: Using StudentSim as the reward signal, not just a benchmark
slides.body: The team trained a chess tutor with reinforcement learning, using StudentSim's reactions as the reward (anchored to an independent Stockfish move-quality signal).
bullets: Tutor RL with StudentSim reward: 90.5% accuracy
Supervised tutor, no RL: 75.7% accuracy
Tutor RL with prompted-GPT-5.4 reward: 71.6% accuracy
Blind human chess experts also rated the StudentSim-trained tutor highest for personalization and guidance quality

slides.title: What this doesn't prove yet
slides.body: The authors are explicit that this is a proof of concept, not a finished tutoring product.
bullets: Only validated end-to-end in chess; writing and math setups exist but ship no comparable numbers
Simulators don't replace human studies for real learning outcomes, safety, or classroom usability
Covers short interactions only — longer learning trajectories are future work
Per-student training data is inherently thin, which is why the two-stage design exists at all

slides.title: Simulated students as a pre-flight check, not a replacement
bullets: StudentSim: one personalized LLM simulator per student, trained from de-identified records
Scored on fidelity to the real student AND responsiveness to tutor guidance
Beat a generic prompted LLM and a domain-specific model on the combined metric
As an RL reward signal, it trained a chess tutor that outperformed supervised and GPT-5.4-reward baselines
Still a proof of concept — real classroom validation is the next step

questions.prompt: Why can't you just prompt a general-purpose LLM to 'act like a student' to test an AI tutor?
options: It's too slow to run at scale
It tends to be too capable, making the tutor look better than it would with a real learner
It can't produce text in the right format
It requires a GPU cluster to run
questions.explanation: The paper's core motivation: generic prompted LLM 'students' respond well to good guidance but don't track any specific learner's actual knowledge gaps, so they overestimate how good a tutor really is.

questions.prompt: What does 'guidance responsiveness' measure in StudentSimEval?
options: How fast the simulator generates a response
Whether the simulator changes its answer after receiving tutor feedback
How closely the simulator's writing style matches a real student's
Whether the simulator ever gives a wrong answer
questions.explanation: It's one of two required axes: a simulator that never updates its answer after feedback is useless for testing whether a tutor's guidance actually helps.

questions.prompt: In the chess reinforcement-learning experiment, which reward source produced the most accurate tutor?
options: A supervised tutor trained with no RL at all
RL with a prompted GPT-5.4 as the reward model
RL with StudentSim as the reward model
They all performed identically
questions.explanation: StudentSim-as-reward reached 90.5% accuracy, beating the no-RL supervised baseline (75.7%) and RL with a GPT-5.4 reward model (71.6%) — and human experts also preferred it.

references.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring — Microsoft Research

posts.title: LSM Trees: Why Databases Trade Read Speed for Write Speed
posts.subtitle: The data structure behind Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB turns random writes into sequential ones — then pays for it later.
posts.summary: Log-Structured Merge trees batch writes in memory and flush them as immutable, sorted files, turning expensive random disk I/O into cheap sequential I/O. The cost shows up later, at read and compaction time — which is exactly the tradeoff that makes LSM trees the default for write-heavy systems like Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB.

slides.title: Why can't a B-tree just handle heavy writes?
slides.body: Every in-place update to a B-tree is a random disk seek. LSM trees sidestep that by never updating in place — they only ever append.

slides.title: Random writes are the bottleneck, not disk capacity
slides.body: A B-tree index updates a key by seeking to its page and rewriting it in place. At high write rates, that's a random I/O per write — and random I/O is 50-100x slower than sequential I/O on spinning disks, and still meaningfully slower on SSDs.
bullets: Each update = seek + read + modify + write a 4-8KB page, even for a tiny key
Write-heavy workloads (logging, metrics, event streams) turn into a wall of random seeks
Page splits and rebalancing add further write amplification on top

slides.title: Buffer in memory, flush as immutable sorted files
slides.body: An LSM tree never rewrites existing data on disk. Writes land in an in-memory sorted structure (the memtable), and once it fills up, it's flushed to disk as a single new immutable, sorted file.
bullets: Write path: append to a write-ahead log (durability) → insert into memtable (e.g. a skip list)
Memtable full → flush the whole thing as one new SSTable (Sorted String Table) — pure sequential write
Old data is never edited in place, only superseded by a newer SSTable
Result: writes become O(1) sequential appends instead of random seeks

slides.title: Reads have to check every layer
slides.body: A key's latest value could be in the memtable, or in any of several SSTables on disk — newest first.
bullets: Check the memtable first (freshest data)
Then check on-disk SSTables, newest to oldest, until the key is found
Each SSTable carries a Bloom filter so a miss can usually be ruled out in microseconds, no disk read needed
Without compaction, a single read could fan out across dozens of SSTables

slides.title: Compaction: merging the layers back down
slides.body: A background process periodically merges SSTables, discarding overwritten and deleted keys, so reads don't have to search an ever-growing pile of files.
bullets: Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra-style): merge same-size SSTables into a bigger one; cheaper writes, bursty disk use
Leveled compaction (RocksDB/LevelDB-style): organize SSTables into levels of exponentially increasing size, merge across levels; steadier disk use, more total write I/O
This re-write of already-written data is 'write amplification' — LSM trees trade it for fast initial writes

slides.title: LSM tree vs. B-tree, in one table
Walking through one write and one read
slides.body: Write key "user:42" = "active": it's appended to the WAL, inserted into the in-memory memtable, and sits there until the memtable fills and flushes as SSTable #17.
bullets: Read "user:42" immediately after: found straight in the memtable, no disk touch
Read it after 5 more flushes: memtable miss → Bloom filter rules out SSTables #18-21 → found in SSTable #17
Delete "user:42": no file is touched — a 'tombstone' marker is written, resolved later during compaction

slides.title: When an LSM tree is the wrong choice
slides.body: The write-speed win isn't free, and some workloads pay more than they gain.
bullets: Read-heavy, write-light workloads: a B-tree's single predictable lookup beats searching multiple SSTables
Strict point-query latency SLAs: compaction can cause unpredictable I/O spikes ('compaction stalls')
Range scans over recently-deleted data: tombstones linger until compaction, adding scan overhead
If you rarely update and mostly do indexed lookups, a B-tree's simplicity usually wins

slides.title: The core tradeoff, in one line
bullets: LSM trees turn random writes into sequential ones by never updating in place
Memtable (RAM) → SSTable (disk, immutable, sorted) is the write path
Bloom filters keep reads fast despite data being spread across many files
Compaction pays back the deferred cost — at the price of background CPU/I/O
Pick LSM for write-heavy systems (Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB); pick B-trees when reads dominate

questions.prompt: What makes LSM tree writes faster than B-tree writes under heavy write load?
options: LSM trees compress data before writing it
LSM trees never write to disk at all
LSM trees turn writes into sequential appends instead of random in-place updates
LSM trees use less memory per key
questions.explanation: A B-tree update means a random seek to rewrite a page in place. An LSM tree buffers writes in memory and flushes them as one sequential write, which is dramatically faster at scale.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a Bloom filter on an SSTable?
options: To compress the SSTable's contents
To quickly rule out that a key exists in that file, avoiding an unnecessary disk read
To sort the keys within the SSTable
To encrypt the data on disk
questions.explanation: Bloom filters give fast, memory-only 'definitely not here' answers. Since a read may have to check many SSTables, this is what keeps point lookups fast despite data being spread across files.

questions.prompt: What is 'write amplification' in the context of LSM trees?
options: Writing the same key to multiple databases for redundancy
The extra disk I/O caused by compaction re-writing data that was already written once
A bug where writes are duplicated accidentally
The memory overhead of the write-ahead log
questions.explanation: Compaction merges and re-writes SSTables to keep read performance in check, which means the same data gets physically written to disk more than once — that deferred cost is the tradeoff for fast initial writes.

posts.title: 211 Designs, 17 Binders: Claude Builds Antivenom Candidates
posts.subtitle: An autonomous protein-design campaign against five scorpion neurotoxins, graded by wet-lab binding data.
posts.summary: Anthropic let Claude run an end-to-end protein-design campaign against five scorpion neurotoxins — picking targets, generating 318,484 candidate binders, choosing which 211 to synthesize, and drafting the report. Wet-lab testing at two independent labs confirmed 17 real binders, including two with nanomolar affinity, validated with the same hit-rate as human-led campaigns.

slides.title: Can an AI Agent Run Its Own Wet-Lab Campaign?
slides.body: Scorpion stings hit over 1.2 million people a year and kill more than 3,250, mostly children with poor medical access. Anthropic tested whether Claude could help design a cheaper path to antivenom, almost entirely on its own.
bullets: Target: five neurotoxins from five regions — Cn2 (Mexico), Ts1 (Brazil), AaH I & AaH II (North Africa), LqhIII (Middle East)
Claude worked ~24 hours autonomously from one prompt, then got four follow-up prompts
Partners: Citrini Research (collaboration), Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience (independent wet-lab testing)

slides.title: Why This Is a Hard Design Problem
slides.body: No de novo binder against any of these five scorpion neurotoxins had been published before — Claude had no template to copy.
bullets: Each toxin binds sodium channels differently, so a binder has to mimic a precise 3D epitope, not just 'something toxin-shaped'
The campaign also tried multitoxin binders — single proteins meant to neutralize 2-3 toxins from the same family at once
Ground truth only exists after real binding assays — there's no simulator that reliably predicts a tight binder before synthesis

slides.title: The Pipeline Claude Ran End-to-End
slides.body: Claude didn't just generate sequences — it ran the whole campaign loop, from structure selection to lab emails.
bullets: Picked toxin structures from the PDB and AlphaFold DB, then chose 5 hotspot residues per toxin to target
Used 12 different design tools to generate 318,484 candidate binders, filtering out anything resembling known proteins
Co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, then selected 180 designs in about 64 hours (~10,000 GPU-hours total)
Drafted the emails sending final sequences to Twist Bioscience, then analyzed the resulting SPR data and wrote the report

slides.title: Single-Toxin vs. Multitoxin Hit Rates
Worked Example: Cn2-B1, the Top Candidate
slides.body: Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2 were two of the seven confirmed Cn2 binders, and the strongest of the whole campaign.
bullets: Both bound Cn2 with single-digit nanomolar affinity (KD), confirmed independently at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience
Hit bar required binding in every replicate at both labs, KD ≤ 1 µM, and no cross-reaction with an unrelated control protein (CLEC12A)
Competition assays suggest Cn2-B1 binds the same or an overlapping epitope as antibody LR, which is already reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice
Existing nanobodies against Cn2 bind sub-nanomolar — so Cn2-B1 is real and promising, but not yet at the best-in-class affinity bar

slides.title: What Worked, What Didn't, What's Next
slides.body: This is a real result with real limits — Anthropic is explicit that this is not an antivenom.
bullets: 17 of 211 designs (8%) were confirmed binders; the single-toxin hit rate (18%) matches typical human-led design campaigns
Every multitoxin design failed to hit the bar for more than one toxin — ambitious generalization is still the harder problem
Only recombinant toxins were tested — no venom-purified toxin, no cell/animal neutralization data yet
Next steps for Cn2-B1: confirm against venom-derived toxin, run patch-clamp functional assays, then test protection in mice

questions.prompt: What was the overall hit rate for single-toxin designs in this campaign?
questions.explanation: 11 of the 60 single-toxin designs (12 per toxin across five toxins) met the binding criteria — an 18% hit rate, which Anthropic notes is in line with typical human-led protein design campaigns.

questions.prompt: How did multitoxin binder designs perform compared to single-toxin designs?
options: They performed better — higher hit rate across all toxins
None of the multitoxin designs met the criteria for binding more than one toxin
They were not attempted in this campaign
They worked equally well for all five toxins
questions.explanation: None of the β-family, α-family, or all-five-toxin designs met the hit criteria for more than one toxin — generalizing a single binder across multiple toxin targets proved much harder than single-toxin design.

questions.prompt: What specifically did Claude do autonomously in this campaign, beyond generating sequences?
options: Nothing — researchers chose targets and thresholds manually
It only ran the final data analysis
It chose target structures and hotspots, set quality thresholds, selected which designs to synthesize, and drafted lab emails and the report
It performed the physical wet-lab binding assays itself
questions.explanation: Claude operated across the whole pipeline — selecting toxin structures and hotspot residues, setting its own filtering thresholds, choosing most of the 180 designs (including the top binder), drafting outreach emails to Twist Bioscience, and writing up the results. The physical assays were run by Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience.

references.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins

posts.title: Magnetar: A zkVM 10-39x Faster, With No Trusted Setup
posts.subtitle: Microsoft Research's new proof system lets any Rust, Go, or C program prove it ran correctly — verified in milliseconds.
posts.summary: Magnetar is Microsoft Research's new zero-knowledge virtual machine: it proves that an ordinary Rust, Go, or C program ran correctly, without a trusted setup and resting only on standard hash functions. It's 10-39x faster than the previous fastest comparable systems and verifies a proof in about 12 milliseconds.

slides.title: A Certificate That a Program Ran Correctly
slides.body: A zero-knowledge proof lets a program return its output plus a short certificate that it executed correctly — checkable in milliseconds, without rerunning it or trusting whoever ran it.
bullets: Released by Microsoft Research (Srinath Setty), October 15, 2026
Builds on over a decade of MSR work making zero-knowledge proofs practical for general-purpose code
Paper: 'Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes'

slides.title: The Three Walls Blocking zkVM Adoption
slides.body: Microsoft frames the barrier as three separate problems, and claims Magnetar addresses all three at once.
bullets: Efficiency: proving execution has historically been orders of magnitude slower than just running the program
Generality/usability: many prior systems require hand-written circuits instead of proving ordinary code as written
Long-term security: many fast systems lean on elliptic curves or novel assumptions that may not survive quantum computers

slides.title: How Magnetar Proves a Program Ran Correctly
slides.body: Magnetar proves execution of the RISC-V RV64 instruction set — so any language with a mature RISC-V compiler is provable without rewriting it as a circuit.
bullets: Built on the sum-check-based approach pioneered by Spartan (2019), which needs no trusted setup
Its processor model builds on Phalanx, exploiting the fact that the same instruction cycle repeats at every step
Long computations are proven 'in pieces and then combined,' drawing on folding techniques from the Nova family
Commitments are hash-based (in the Brakedown lineage) — verification is mostly hash evaluations and binary-field arithmetic

slides.title: Magnetar vs. Prior zkVMs (as reported)
Worked Example: Proving a Token Transfer
slides.body: Microsoft's own benchmark: proving correct execution of a token transfer inside a small EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) interpreter.
bullets: The program is ordinary interpreter code — no manual circuit design needed, since Magnetar proves the compiled RISC-V binary directly
On this benchmark, Magnetar ran more than 300x faster than the two (unnamed) baseline systems it was compared against
The resulting proof verifies in ~12 ms — fast enough to check on every transaction without re-executing it
Same pattern generalizes to proving a ledger stayed consistent, or that a business/data pipeline ran its stated logic

slides.title: What This Changes, and What's Still Open
slides.body: Magnetar makes 'prove it ran correctly' practical for ordinary code — but it isn't a drop-in privacy tool for every use case.
bullets: Big win: no circuit rewrites — compile existing Rust/Go/C to RISC-V and prove the binary as-is
Hash-only security means the post-quantum story is simpler, but the construction trades on less battle-tested commitment schemes than pairing-based SNARKs
The post doesn't name the specific competing zkVMs in its benchmarks or publish proof sizes — treat the speedup numbers as Microsoft's own, pending independent replication
Not yet a public code release — current access is via contact for ZKP use cases, not an open-source repo

questions.prompt: What cryptographic assumption does Magnetar rely on for its security?
options: Elliptic-curve pairings
Lattice-based cryptography
Only a standard hash function (e.g. SHA-256 or SHA-3) — no trusted setup, no elliptic curves
A novel, unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes
questions.explanation: Magnetar's design deliberately avoids elliptic curves, lattices, and novel conjectures, relying only on standard hash functions — which is also why it's described as post-quantum.

questions.prompt: Why can Magnetar prove ordinary Rust, Go, or C programs without rewriting them as circuits?
options: It doesn't — every program still needs a hand-written circuit
It proves execution of the compiled RISC-V (RV64) instruction stream, so any language with a RISC-V compiler is provable as-is
It only supports a custom DSL designed for Magnetar
It interprets Python bytecode directly
questions.explanation: Magnetar operates at the RISC-V instruction-set level, so normal toolchains compile Rust/Go/C down to RISC-V and Magnetar proves that binary executed correctly — no circuit design required.

questions.prompt: On the reported 15-benchmark comparison, how much faster is Magnetar than the prior fastest comparable zkVMs, on average?
options: 2x
questions.explanation: Microsoft reports a 10-39x average speedup across 15 benchmarks against the fastest existing comparable zkVMs on the same machine, with one token-transfer benchmark showing a 300x+ gap.

posts.title: GraphRAG: When Flat Retrieval Can't Answer the Question
posts.subtitle: Why some questions need a knowledge graph and community summaries instead of just the nearest chunks.
posts.summary: Standard RAG retrieves the top-k chunks most similar to a query — great for 'what does X say,' terrible for 'what connects X, Y, and Z across the whole corpus.' GraphRAG fixes this by extracting entities and relationships into a knowledge graph, clustering them into communities, and pre-summarizing each community so broad, corpus-wide questions have something to retrieve against.

slides.title: The Question Flat RAG Can't Answer
slides.body: Vector and hybrid RAG are built around one premise: the answer lives in a handful of chunks that are each individually similar to the query.
bullets: That premise holds for 'what is our refund policy' — it breaks for 'what are the main themes across all 10,000 support tickets this quarter'
No single chunk is similar to a question about the whole corpus, so top-k retrieval returns nothing useful
GraphRAG (popularized by Microsoft Research) restructures the corpus itself, instead of just retrieving from it differently

slides.title: Why Chunk-Level Retrieval Breaks on 'Global' Questions
slides.body: Standard RAG is a local retrieval method — it's blind to structure that only exists across many documents.
bullets: Multi-hop questions ('how is Company A connected to Company B') need facts stitched from several far-apart chunks the retriever never pulls together
Thematic/aggregation questions ('summarize the main complaints') have no single matching passage, because the answer is a pattern, not a fact
More context doesn't fix it — stuffing in more top-k chunks just adds noise, since relevance-to-query isn't the same as relevance-to-theme

slides.title: The Mechanism: Build a Graph, Then Summarize Communities
slides.body: GraphRAG is an indexing-time investment that pays off at query time for exactly the questions flat RAG can't handle.
bullets: Step 1 — Extraction: an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities (people, orgs, concepts) and the relationships between them
Step 2 — Graph construction: entities become nodes, relationships become edges, forming a knowledge graph over the whole corpus
Step 3 — Community detection: a clustering algorithm (e.g. Leiden) groups densely-connected nodes into hierarchical communities
Step 4 — Community summarization: an LLM pre-writes a summary for each community, at multiple levels of granularity

slides.title: Two Query Modes, Not One
slides.body: GraphRAG systems typically expose both a local and a global search mode, and route between them.
bullets: Local search: for a specific-entity question, retrieve that entity's node, its neighbors, and their source chunks — this looks a lot like regular RAG, just graph-aware
Global search: for a thematic question, retrieve the relevant pre-written community summaries instead of raw chunks, then map-reduce an answer across them
The LLM never has to re-discover corpus-wide structure at query time — community summarization already did that work offline

slides.title: Flat (Hybrid) RAG vs. GraphRAG

rows: Higher for global search (map-reduce over summaries)
Re-run extraction/clustering as the graph evolves

slides.title: Worked Example: An M&A Due-Diligence Corpus
slides.body: A legal team ingests thousands of contracts, filings, and emails and asks two very different questions.
bullets: "What termination clause applies to the Acme supply contract?" — a local question. The graph's Acme node and its contract-chunk neighbors answer it directly, same as good hybrid RAG would
"Which entities across all these documents have overlapping board members or shared subsidiaries?" — a global/thematic question. No single chunk contains that answer
GraphRAG answers the second question by surfacing the community that clustered those entities together, with a summary already written describing the shared ownership pattern
Flat RAG would need the user to already know which documents to compare — GraphRAG discovered the connection during indexing

slides.title: When GraphRAG Is Worth the Extra Pipeline
slides.body: GraphRAG trades a much more expensive indexing phase for the ability to answer questions flat retrieval structurally cannot.
bullets: Use it when users actually ask broad, thematic, or multi-hop questions over a large, interconnected corpus — not just lookup queries
Skip it for small or shallow corpora, or workloads that are 95% specific-fact lookups — hybrid RAG is cheaper and plenty good enough
Budget for it: entity/relationship extraction and community summarization both run an LLM over the entire corpus at index time, which costs real money and time
It's not a replacement for hybrid RAG — most production systems route local questions to standard retrieval and only invoke the graph for global ones

questions.prompt: What kind of question does flat (chunk-level) RAG struggle with most?
options: Specific fact lookups like 'what is our refund policy'
Broad, thematic, or multi-hop questions where the answer is spread across many documents
Questions about a single short document
Questions with exact keyword matches
questions.explanation: Flat RAG retrieves chunks individually similar to the query — it has no mechanism for answering questions whose answer is a pattern or connection spanning many documents, since no single chunk 'is' the answer.

questions.prompt: In GraphRAG, what is a 'community' and why does it matter?
options: A random sample of chunks used for testing
A cluster of densely-connected entities in the knowledge graph, pre-summarized so global/thematic queries have something concrete to retrieve
A group of users who share search history
A backup copy of the vector index
questions.explanation: Community detection (e.g. via the Leiden algorithm) groups related entities together, and pre-writing a summary for each community at index time is what lets global queries retrieve a ready-made answer instead of requiring the LLM to synthesize corpus-wide structure on the fly.

questions.prompt: Why wouldn't a team building a simple FAQ bot over 300 short articles want GraphRAG?
options: GraphRAG only works with images
The corpus is small and shallow, so hybrid RAG already answers lookup-style questions well without the extra extraction/clustering cost
GraphRAG requires a GPU cluster to even query
FAQ bots can't use knowledge graphs at all
questions.explanation: GraphRAG's value comes from handling corpus-wide, multi-hop questions over large interconnected data — for a small FAQ corpus where nearly every question is a direct lookup, the extra indexing cost (LLM-driven entity extraction and community summarization) doesn't pay for itself.

posts.title: MCP Primitives: Tools, Resources, and Prompts Aren't the Same
posts.subtitle: The Model Context Protocol gives servers three distinct ways to reach an AI app — collapsing them into 'just add a tool' wastes tokens and breaks clients.
posts.summary: MCP doesn't define one generic way for servers to expose capabilities — it defines three, each controlled by a different party: Tools the model calls, Resources the application attaches, and Prompts the user explicitly invokes. Treating them as interchangeable burns model turns on things that should've been free context and blows up the function-calling schema the model has to read every turn.

slides.title: A Server That Exposes Everything as a 'Tool' Is Doing It Wrong
bullets: MCP defines three server-side primitives — Tools, Resources, Prompts — plus Sampling and Elicitation, which flow server-to-client instead
Each primitive has a different controller: the model, the host application, or the human user — mixing them up has a real cost in tokens and turns

slides.title: "Just Add It as a Tool" Ignores Who's Supposed to Decide
slides.body: Most MCP servers get built by reaching for tools/call for everything, because it's the primitive everyone understands from function calling.
bullets: A read-only lookup (list open PRs, fetch a README) exposed as a Tool forces the model to spend a turn and tokens deciding to call it, even when the answer was known before the conversation started
Dumping static reference data into a Tool's response also means it competes with every other tool's JSON schema for space in the model's context on every single turn
The fix isn't a coding convention — MCP already separates these by who initiates them, and the spec expects servers to pick the right one

slides.title: Three Primitives, Three Different Controllers
bullets: Tools — model-controlled: callable functions with a JSON schema, discovered via tools/list and invoked via tools/call. The LLM decides when and with what arguments, same shape as ordinary function calling — e.g. create_pull_request(repo, head, base, title)

Resources — application-controlled: addressable data behind a URI, discovered via resources/list and fetched via resources/read. The host app, not the model, decides what to attach to context — e.g. repo://acme/widgets/README.md, opened automatically when a user opens that repo

Prompts — user-controlled: reusable message templates with arguments, discovered via prompts/list and expanded via prompts/get. A human explicitly triggers them, like a slash command — e.g. /review-pr 482

slides.title: JSON-RPC Underneath, With Capability Negotiation First
slides.body: Every MCP message is JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or streamable HTTP — the primitives are just a convention for which methods a server implements.
bullets: On connect, client and server exchange an initialize handshake declaring capabilities — which of tools/resources/prompts/sampling they support, and whether resources support subscribe for change notifications
A client that skips this and calls tools/call on a server with no tools capability gets a protocol error, not an empty list

Later spec revisions added Elicitation (server asks the user, mid-task, for missing information) and kept Sampling (server asks the client's own model for a completion) as the two primitives that run server-to-client instead of client-to-server

slides.title: One GitHub MCP Server, Three Primitives in Use
slides.body: A coding agent connects to a GitHub MCP server while a developer is fixing a bug in acme/widgets.
bullets: Resource: the IDE auto-attaches repo://acme/widgets/README.md and the open file's diff as context the moment the workspace opens — no model decision, no tokens spent deciding, just background context

Prompt: the developer types /review-pr 482 — the server expands that into a fully-formed message bundling the diff, existing review comments, and a checklist, independent of anything the model would've chosen to fetch
Tool: mid-task, the agent decides on its own that it needs to open a new PR, so it calls create_pull_request(repo, head, base, title) with arguments it fills in from the conversation

slides.title: Tools vs. Resources vs. Prompts vs. Sampling

rows: Take an action with side effects
Ask the client's LLM for a completion

slides.title: Where This Goes Wrong in Practice
bullets: Modeling a read-only lookup as a Tool instead of a Resource costs a model turn and tokens for something the host could've attached upfront for free
Skipping mimeType and annotations on Resources breaks clients that filter or render by content type — they see an opaque blob instead of markdown or JSON

One tool per CRUD field (get_title, get_status, get_assignee...) multiplies the function-calling schema the model re-reads every single turn — context cost scales with how many tools exist, not how many get used
The spec says a client SHOULD always let a human approve a Sampling request before it's sent — skipping that turns a data server into an unsupervised sub-agent making its own LLM calls

slides.title: Pick the Primitive by Who Should Decide, Not by What's Easiest
bullets: Tools are for actions the model should decide to take mid-task; Resources are for context the application already knows to attach; Prompts are for workflows a human explicitly triggers
Capability negotiation at connect time means a client should never assume a server supports a primitive it hasn't advertised
Fewer, coarser Tools beat many fine-grained ones — every tool's schema costs context on every turn, whether or not the model ever calls it

questions.prompt: In MCP, who decides when a Tool actually gets called?
options: The model, mid-conversation, the same way it decides to make any function call
The host application, before the conversation starts
The human user, by typing a slash command
The MCP server itself, on a fixed schedule
questions.explanation: Tools are the model-controlled primitive: the LLM decides when to invoke tools/call and with what arguments, just like ordinary function calling. That's what distinguishes them from Resources (app-controlled) and Prompts (user-controlled).

questions.prompt: What's the practical downside of exposing a read-only data lookup as a Tool instead of a Resource?
options: It forces the model to spend a turn and tokens deciding to call it, when the host application could have attached that data to context directly
Tools can only return plain text, never structured data
Resources are deprecated in the current MCP spec
Tools cannot be discovered by the client at all
questions.explanation: Resources are meant for context the application already knows to attach — no model decision required. Routing the same data through a Tool means the model has to notice it needs the data, decide to call the tool, and wait for the round trip, all of which costs tokens and latency for nothing.

questions.prompt: What has to happen before a client can safely call any of a server's tools, resources, or prompts?
options: A capability negotiation during the initialize handshake, so the client knows which primitives the server actually supports
The user must manually approve every primitive the server exposes
The server must first call the client's sampling endpoint
Nothing — all MCP servers are required to support every primitive
questions.explanation: MCP connections start with an initialize exchange where client and server declare their capabilities. A client that calls, say, tools/call against a server that never advertised a tools capability gets a protocol error rather than a graceful empty response.
